column1: Give the five adjectives the slide applies to wicked problems.
column2: Unsolvable, undefinable, unverifiable, unique, uncertain.

column1: Define a wicked problem.
column2: An issue that resists a complete or simple solution; it can be ameliorated but not solved, and amelioration may create new problems.

column1: Who originated the term "wicked problem", and when?
column2: Rittel and Webber, 1973.

column1: How many characteristics of wicked problems did the original paper set out?
column2: Ten.

column1: What distinguishes a complex problem from a wicked one?
column2: A complex problem is hard but may have an optimal solution; a wicked one resists complete solution.

column1: What defines a "long" problem?
column2: Its timeframe.

column1: Give the lecture's example of a complex but not wicked problem.
column2: The City Rail Link - testing air conditioning, alarms, capacity and passenger flow optimisation.

column1: Why is Western society said to struggle with long problems?
column2: It is set up to solve short-term problems; long problems outlast governments and quarterly business reporting.

column1: Are most ENGGEN403 problems wicked, complex or long?
column2: Both complex and long, as well as wicked.

column1: Give the renewables example of a wicked problem.
column2: Shifting from fossil fuels to renewables creates job losses, weather-dependent supply, battery storage problems, lithium toxicity, recycling difficulty and critical-mineral supply-chain issues.

column1: What is the "wicked signature" shown by the renewables example?
column2: The fix worked and still generated an entirely new problem set.

column1: Why is recovering critical minerals from batteries a problem?
column2: Components are muddled together, and it costs more to extract them than to mine them from the ground.

column1: What replaces "solve" as the goal for a wicked problem?
column2: Ameliorate - shift the system in the right direction even without a complete solution.

column1: What shape should a systems recommendation take?
column2: We understand the system well enough to predict its behaviour; do this, and it will shift the system to there.

column1: What three things does systems thinking provide?
column2: Context, language and tools.

column1: In the Portland State map, what are the two overlapping circles?
column2: Systems research and systems practice.

column1: What sits in the overlap of the Portland State map?
column2: Systems methodology - containing systems thinking, and computer modelling and simulation.

column1: Name three items on the systems research side of the Portland State map.
column2: Complexity theory, chaos theory, fractals (also complex adaptive systems and computational intelligence).

column1: Name three items on the systems practice side of the Portland State map.
column2: Systems engineering, systems analysis, systems management (also systems approach to problem solving).

column1: Define systems methodology.
column2: A process that uses a diverse group with systems thinking tools to get from initial chaos to an agreed preliminary definition of the problem, then takes steps to develop an improvement.

column1: What comes before improving the problem, in systems methodology?
column2: Agreeing a preliminary definition of what the problem actually is.

column1: How does Morganelli (2024) frame systems thinking?
column2: As a mindset more than a prescribed practice.

column1: How does Michael Goodman frame systems thinking?
column2: As more than a collection of tools and methods - an underlying philosophy.

column1: What is meant by "Systems Thinking is Soft Operations Research"?
column2: It is about how you are going to get things done.

column1: Give Arnold and Wade's definition of systems thinking.
column2: A set of synergistic analytic skills used to improve the capability of identifying and understanding systems, predicting their behaviours, and devising modifications to produce desired effects.

column1: What three capabilities does the Arnold and Wade definition name in order?
column2: Identify and understand systems, predict their behaviour, devise modifications.

column1: State the lecturer's preferred definition of a system.
column2: A set of connected parts that together form a cohesive whole.

column1: Give the Hall and Fagen (1956) definition of a system.
column2: A set of objects together with relationships between the objects and between their attributes.

column1: What is the "environment" in Hall and Fagen's definition?
column2: The set of all objects whose attribute changes affect the system, and those whose attributes are changed by the system's behaviour.

column1: Why is the clunky Hall and Fagen definition still useful?
column2: As a scoping checklist: what is in the system, what is out, and what is in the environment.

column1: Name the three common features every system has.
column2: Elements, interconnections, and purpose.

column1: What check tells you that you have over-simplified a system?
column2: Ask whether you still have definable elements, interconnected, whose interconnections change the properties, with an overall purpose. If not, it is no longer a system.

column1: What is described as "always" the key issue in systems work?
column2: The boundary - deciding what to consider and what to leave out.

column1: What is the project-management synonym for the system boundary?
column2: In scope versus out of scope.

column1: Name the three labels on the boundary diagram.
column2: Surroundings, boundary, and system.

column1: Give the metabolic map boundary dilemma.
column2: Whether to draw the boundary around lysine biosynthesis, amino acid biosynthesis, glucose metabolism, or the Krebs cycle.

column1: What are New Zealand's "three waters", and why is the boundary hard?
column2: Fresh water, wastewater and stormwater - three separate systems that all connect, and near an estuary seawater connects too.

column1: What is the practical constraint on how wide you draw a boundary?
column2: How big a problem you can actually keep in your heads and still move forward.

column1: Define an emergent property.
column2: A property of the whole system that could not have been predicted from the individual components.

column1: What do emergent properties depend on besides the components?
column2: The relationships between components, and to an extent the inputs and outputs.

column1: What are the two names used for the same idea about a system's overall behaviour?
column2: Emergent property, and purpose.

column1: Give three different purposes for the musculoskeletal system.
column2: A biologist sees movement and motion; a physiotherapist sees running faster; a coach sees which muscle to strengthen and which ligament not to snap.

column1: What does the musculoskeletal example show about purpose?
column2: Purpose is assigned by the framing and the observer, not discovered in the parts.

column1: What does it mean that systems nest?
column2: The cardiovascular system is self-contained but sits inside the body, and zooming down reveals the metabolic map.

column1: Give the example of a system's purpose drifting over time.
column2: Research institutes set up to break down silos eventually shift to keeping their funding, and become silos themselves.

column1: What is the scoping warning that follows from purpose drift?
column2: The purpose you think a system was set up for may not be the purpose it ended up with; read purpose off current behaviour.

column1: Describe the metabolic map inversion.
column2: Elements and interconnections were swapped: enzymes became the elements and molecules became the interconnections, treated as signals.

column1: Why was the metabolic map conventionally drawn with molecules as elements?
column2: Historical accident - molecules were discovered before enzymes.

column1: What did the metabolic map inversion achieve?
column2: Complexity shrank: enzymes clustered together and only a few signals were needed to understand it.

column1: What general move does the metabolic map inversion suggest?
column2: If a system map is unmanageably tangled, try swapping what you treat as elements and what you treat as interconnections.

column1: How does the stakeholder set differ between ENGGEN303 and ENGGEN403?
column2: 303 was a business and its customers or suppliers; 403 adds the public, local and central government, NGOs, iwi and immigrant communities.

column1: Why is stakeholder disagreement diagnostic?
column2: If all stakeholders wanted the same thing it would be a simple problem, not a wicked one.

column1: Name three kinds of power operating in a government-level system.
column2: Structural power (ministers, mayors), influence without formal power (lobbyists, media), and affected communities with little power.

column1: Why do power dynamics decide whether your recommendations work?
column2: They determine whether recommendations move the problem forward or get caught up in a fight when they land.

column1: What is said about engineers' skill set for wicked problems?
column2: It is a useful skill set, but not the only one; these problems need collaboration across disciplines.

column1: What should a team do about fast thinkers who jump to a solution?
column2: Take a breath and also listen to the quieter deep thinkers who come in later.

column1: What should teams expect about their own progress on a systems problem?
column2: To make progress, then find a fundamental flaw in their thinking, and have to reset.

column1: What is the warning about time-boxing the chaos?
column2: Do not spend the whole week arguing about how to frame the problem statement.

column1: What is the calibration test for whether you are thinking hard enough?
column2: If it is not making your head hurt, you are not thinking about it hard enough.

column1: What is the required reading, and how much?
column2: Thinking in Systems - at least the first two chapters, ahead of Lecture 8.
